That's the beauty of the juice weasel: if it runs fine on 1.9.4, then run it on 1.9.4. The best way to set your apps up in Wine is to configure a separate Wine prefix for each application. This gives you the flexibility to run a different version of Wine and different, very specific, Windows settings for each application. The drive space consumption for setting things up this way is negligible, and it saves you a lot of headache in the long run. If you have access to PlayOnLinux, I highly recommend it, because it automates a lot of this.

Wait what? Is there a reason why 1.9.9 wouldn't work and 1.9.4 would? Also, what does configuring a separate WINE prefix for each application entail? I've been doing all of my configuration thus far through Winetricks, or should I just start doing some searching for that?

I do have access to PlayOnLinux, but it didn't have any of the games that I'm having trouble with in the list of games it deals with.

Various reasons, but the most prominent is that 1.8.2 is actually the stable release, and if you're running 1.9.9, then you're running a development release. A lot of distros don't make this entirely clear when you do a yum/apt-get/pkg install wine*. But that's why some functionality that is in, say 1.9.4, might be missing in 1.9.9, or just broken because of and addition that clobbered it.

I haven't used Winetricks in forever, so my info may be a bit old, but as I recall, it should be as simple as setting up separate virtual drives or directories for your applications and specifying the Wine version you want to run inside that container.

For PlayOnLinux, don't pay much attention to what's available via the install scripts. There should be a link on the install window to do a custom install, and all the options will be presented to you: create a new Wine prefix; download a new Wine version or use an existing one; install additional software within the container; etc. All nice and clicky... keeps people happy.
